claims.text: Slower post-synthesis thermal ramp rates are the primary factor enabling near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles to preserve structural and chemical stability at high temperatures.
Slower thermal ramps reduce thermal gradients during annealing.
Reduced thermal gradients limit elemental interdiffusion.
Limiting elemental interdiffusion hinders the onset of phase separation.
Rapid thermal ramping produces uneven thermal exposure.
Rapid thermal ramping accelerates microphase segregation.
Microphase segregation degrades structural and chemical homogeneity.
Structural and chemical homogeneity is essential for sustained operational performance.
Slow-ramped nanoparticles will retain a homogeneous solid-solution structure better than rapidly ramped nanoparticles.
Retention of a homogeneous solid solution after slow ramping will be indicated by sharper X-ray diffraction peaks.
Slow-ramped nanoparticles will show more uniform elemental maps than rapidly treated nanoparticles.
Rapidly treated nanoparticles are expected to exhibit additional phases or compositional gradients.
Nanoparticles initially homogeneous under a moderate thermal ramp may develop phase separation during high-temperature exposure.
The proposed ramp-rate mechanism applies across catalytic temperatures of 773–1173 K and thermoelectric temperatures of 473–1923 K.
The effect of thermal ramp rate may depend on the exact alloy system, departure from equiatomic composition, fabrication method, and detailed ramp profile.
